articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says indirect talks with U.S. on ceasefire proposal continue
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says indirect talks with U.S. on ceasefire proposal continue
articles.content_orig:
A Qatari aircraft arrived in Tehran Tuesday just minutes after a plane carrying Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, departed. The Qatari plane left the Iranian capital approximately 30 minutes later, according to aviation tracking data cited by Iran's semi-official Fars News agency.
The aircraft's short stay raised questions about whether it might have been carrying a diplomatic message amid ongoing indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Qatar is among the nations that have acted as mediators between the two sides for months.
No information about the aircraft's passengers or why it was in Tehran for only half an hour were provided in the Fars report.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they had targeted a Saudi military operations room at Badr Camp in Aden, in southwest Yemen, with a ballistic missile on Wednesday.
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, in a post on X , called the strike a direct hit.
"Our armed forces successfully targeted the enemy Saudi operations room at Badr Camp in Aden with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate and direct," he said.
Aden is the de facto seat of power of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which was forced to decamp after the Houthis occupied the national capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.
The attack claimed by the Houthis Wednesday was the third in a week on Aden.
A police official in Aden told the French news agency AFP earlier that there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile." Two other security sources told AFP the strike targeted a site near the city's airport.
A senior official from Iran's Revolutionary Guard threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure comes under attack.
Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani, the IRGC's deputy for political affairs, warned Iran would use its full capabilities to retaliate if the U.S. and its allies launch new attacks against Iranian infrastructure. He said various investments and assets, including undersea cables carrying internet data in the strategic waterway, could be among the targets of Iranian retaliation if hostilities resume.
"The Americans and their allies have significant investments, and if they want to damage our infrastructure, it is natural that the Islamic Republic will use all its capabilities and easily destroy their investments and assets, including the internet cables that pass beneath the waters of the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
Analysts say cutting the cables in the waterway would most likely affect internet connectivity in Persian Gulf countries .
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Tehran and Washington were still engaged in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal presented by Iran in September.
Araghchi said the U.S. was seeking to add further clauses to the Iranian proposal, which Mr. Trump rejected last month.
The proposal called for the end of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil sales, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
He said Pakistan and Qatar were among the nations facilitating the indirect talks between Iran and the U.S., as they have been for months.
"The negotiating table remains in place," Araghchi said. "It is the American side that is closing the path, not Iran."
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.
"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."
The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it would not return to the negotiating table unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."
"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."

articles.title_orig: Kremlin says China, Russia, US open to trilateral talks at APEC summit
articles.title_zh: Kremlin says China, Russia, US open to trilateral talks at APEC summit
articles.content_orig:
Moscow also freed retired US teacher Stephen Hubbard following a meeting between the Russian leader and Trump’s envoy Witkoff
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since second world war.
The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
President Donald Trump confirmed the release in a social media post, saying the United States was not required to give anything in return.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and was later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and US-based lawyer question.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Opens Higher; SpaceX Shares Surge on Tesla Deal Talks — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Opens Higher; SpaceX Shares Surge on Tesla Deal Talks — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX- Tesla merger.
The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion.
Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier.
On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday.
Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab , Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.
SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG.
"We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release.
Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink , and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure.
The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year.
Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note.
"Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.
They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."
The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.
Correction: Bret Johnsen is chief financial officer at SpaceX. An earlier version misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
articles.title_zh: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
articles.content_orig:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
CNBC has reached out to Meta for comment on the penalty order.
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Judge Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico state Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Raúl Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child-safety related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

articles.title_orig: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.title_zh: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.content_orig:
Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.
The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.
Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.
A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.
"We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC.
"We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time."
The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.
Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.
Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.
A Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it.
Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain".
Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.
While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".
Meanwhile, one person on Instagram questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing.
"I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said.
"These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."

articles.title_orig: Australian politician who was hit by car has lost both legs
articles.title_zh: Australian politician who was hit by car has lost both legs
articles.content_orig:
Watch: 'Her heart and her mind are in good shape', husband of Helen Haines says
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.
Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.
Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.
Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.
"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."
He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.
"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.
Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.
He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
Watch: BBC inside court with man charged with Australian MP attack
In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.
Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.
"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."
Phil and Helen Haines have been married for nearly 40 years - next month is their anniversary
Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.
Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.
Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".
The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.
Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.
"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.
"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.
Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.
Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.
The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.
In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.
There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.
Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.
Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.
Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.
Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".
"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.
"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

articles.title_orig: SpaceX will attempt to reach weekly Starship launches by early 2027
articles.title_zh: SpaceX will attempt to reach weekly Starship launches by early 2027
articles.content_orig:
In its current iteration, SpaceX is largely a data company seeking to provide enormous amounts of compute for artificial intelligence. During an earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, company officials spent much of their time discussing ambitious plans to roll out up to 10 GW of compute in 2027—on the ground.
Gone are the days of aspirational talk about sending humans to Mars and settling the red planet. Now it is almost all about artificial intelligence and the data needed to support its expansion. However, the company’s long-term ambitions to provide data services from space, initially with the Starlink Internet constellation and eventually through the “Starmind” data center constellation, still rely on an actual rocket.
That would be the Starship vehicle, and during the earnings call, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and the company’s president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, provided new performance targets for the vehicle.
It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test, Musk said, to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight.
Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight.
One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico.
“We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” Shotwell said.
As for what comes after this test flight, Shotwell said SpaceX would attempt to refly a Starship upper stage “early” next year. The company will also seek to complete a long-delayed refueling test of Starship early in 2027. This Starship-to-Starship refueling demonstration is an important milestone for SpaceX and NASA to prove the viability of Starship being refueled in low-Earth orbit for lunar missions.
Refueling on this scale has never been done before, and the company needs to get data on the efficiency of such transfers and the rate of boil-off of liquid oxygen and methane in space. This data will refine projections for how many launches are needed to support a Starship landing on the Moon for NASA as part of the Artemis Program.
For SpaceX, the near-term priority is reaching a high flight cadence for Starship and pushing the boundaries of vehicle reuse to enable it.
Musk, who often offers hyper-optimistic timeframes, said he expects Starship to reach a “weekly” flight cadence during the first half of 2027 and to launch twice weekly during the second half of the year. The key will be how much Starship can be reused.
“The rate at which we launch Starship will increase dramatically as we solve rapid and complete reusability,” Musk said. “At first there will be a little bit of refurbishment that’s needed between each flight, and we’ll iron out the need for any refurbishment such that you can immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.”
That’s the vision, at least. Achieving complete reusability with an orbital rocket has never been done before, so SpaceX’s engineering team will undoubtedly face some significant hurdles. Over time, however, they are likely to get close to the vision of launching, landing, and reflying rockets.
SpaceX will largely focus on its own payloads in 2027 with the Starship rocket. Shotwell said the company would continue launching Starlink V3 satellites, the second generation of “mobile” satellites that deliver direct-to-cell connectivity, as well as Starmind data center prototypes, next year. During the earnings call, neither Musk nor Shotwell addressed, nor were asked by financial analysts, about the controversial throttling of Starlink capabilities for Ukraine in its war with Russia.

We’re just weeks away from the release of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV . Prepare for your return to Kronos with an epic, nine-minute trailer:
This video is hosted on a third party website, which may be using cookies. To see it, you need to accept cookies by clicking on the button below. You can change your preferences at any time by clicking Cookie Settings at the bottom of any Warhammer Community page.
In the fourth installment of the legendary Warhammer 40,000 real-time strategy game series, you can take control of four factions – the Space Marines of the Blood Ravens and Dark Angels , Orks, Necrons, and Adeptus Mechanicus – across four campaigns comprising more than 70 thrilling missions.
In addition to the campaigns, there’s a Skirmish mode, with dozens of customisable settings, four game types, and support for up to five AI opponents, where you can hone your skills before taking the battle online across 30 multiplayer maps.
Fan-favourite co-op survival mode The Last Stand is back, where you and two allies must hold the line against relentless waves of enemies. Choose from five heroes and assemble your strike force of companion units, bringing new layers of strategic depth to every run.
Whichever mode you like to play, the enhanced Painter tool means you can make every army your own. Choose from dozens of presets or create your own schemes with choices of colours, decals, and wargear – for the first time, you have complete creative control to paint your units’ armour and equipment piece-by-piece.
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is due for release on 3 December 2026, but if you can’t wait until then, the Commander Edition gives players early access three days ahead of the main release. Pre-order either edition now to get a 10% discount, and prepare to begin the fight for Kronus anew.

The letter asks Google CEO Sundar Pichai to respond by Nov. 2 on what the company knows about AI's effect on students
Kevin Carter / Getty Images
Sens. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, sent a letter to Google $GOOGL CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect the mental health of kids and their growth as learners, according to The Wall Street Journal .
The senators wrote that they have "grave concern" that Google 's "aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation." They set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to reply.
The letter asks Pichai how much Google understands about the ways its AI tools might harm children, why AI features were made the default setting on school devices, which worries districts, teachers and parents have voiced about students leaning on AI academically and emotionally, and which promotions Google has used to broaden the use of AI in schools.
" Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price," the senators wrote, according to The Wall Street Journal. "We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples' best interest."
The letter cites a September Wall Street Journal investigation. Drawing on more than 60 conversations with educators, school officials, parents, students and clinicians, the investigation found that many students have grown emotionally and academically reliant on Google 's AI tools, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Journal also spoke with current and former Google staff and examined the company's research papers, which showed that Google 's own researchers have cautioned that the technology can carry heightened risks for children and may cause cognitive and emotional harm, according to The Wall Street Journal.
A Google spokesperson pointed The Wall Street Journal to a statement the company issued previously, which read “teachers around the world use our technology every day because it solves real classroom challenges and helps improve learning outcomes.” The statement said Google develops its products by working alongside educators and leaves teachers and administrators in charge of how they are used. Google has said it promotes critical thinking and built safeguards aimed at users younger than 18, among them steps meant to head off emotional dependence, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Slipping test scores have driven a backlash against classroom screen time among people of all political stripes, according to The Wall Street Journal. Parent anger has prompted districts such as New York City and Los Angeles to suspend AI use by students in their classrooms through moratoriums, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Chromebooks make up roughly 59% of the devices in U.S. schools, according to Crypto Briefing . By early October, Google had extended access to its Gemini student hub to every K-12 user on Google Workspace for Education, according to Crypto Briefing.
In a July report, Common Sense Media found that the AI tools built into Google Search, such as AI Overview and AI Mode, present an “unacceptable risk” to kids, according to Crypto Briefing. A Senate HELP subcommittee convened on Oct. 9 to examine how AI is affecting K-12 education, according to Crypto Briefing.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.title_zh: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.content_orig:
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.
In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.
Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.
The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.
A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.
The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.
K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.
On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.
In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.
In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.
Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.
The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.
In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”
In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.
“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

articles.title_orig: Meta earnings live updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction
articles.title_zh: Meta earnings live updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction
articles.content_orig:
Meta is slated to report third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, and investors will be looking for signs that the company's latest artificial intelligence efforts will bolster future sales.
Here's what analysts polled by LSEG are expecting:
It's been a big quarter for Mark Zuckerberg's company due to the initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool that debuted in September and shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022.
Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, including Muse Wonder , which was released last Monday.
Wall Street will likely be monitoring for whether Meta plans to increase its data center-related capital expenditures, or capex, to further develop the underlying computing infrastructure needed to power AI agents and foundation models.
The company revealed in July during its second-quarter earnings that it narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to come in between $130 billion and $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its prior range. All that spending resulted in Meta's free cash flow in the period shrinking to $784 million from $8.55 billion in the same quarter a year earlier.
Analysts expect Meta's capex to swell to $196.3 billion in 2027, according to FactSet.
Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, is expected to come in at 3.65 billion, according to StreetAccount, almost flat from the prior quarter. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram.
The Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago continues to haunt Zuckerberg and his social media empire.
New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew imposed a $25 billion penalty on Meta today over a state data privacy case that derived from 2018 privacy revelations.  The fine, revealed in a court filing, came after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse determined that the company formally known as Facebook should be held liable for misleading New Mexico residents about its data handling practices and methods to prevent harmful information from spreading on its family of apps.
Although New Mexico was awarded $219.5 billion, based on the social media company committing over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, the judge reduced that figure to $25 billion.
"Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, judge Mathew wrote in the filing, regarding the company's then pledge to examine the "data misuse."
Analysts at Bank of America wrote in a note published Friday that they expect Meta to post a sales beat, with revenue of $63.8 billion, based in part on the firm's "solid ad checks" with brands and companies that helps determine the health of the digital ad market.
The analysts don't expect Muse to contribute significantly to Meta's overall business for the rest of this year and 2027 and instead "will consume capacity w/o near-term revs.," meaning that the company's AI agent efforts will take some time to grow into something bigger.
Morgan Stanley analysts agree that Meta's Muse AI agent initiatives won't generate big sales anytime soon, and while they said in a Sunday research note that they are "bullish," they "encourage investors to keep reasonable adoption rates in perspective."
The analysts explained that it takes a long time for new technology habits and behaviors to normalize. In 2000, when the e-commerce boom was just five years deep, for instance, the analysts noted that online retail "only made up 4% of adj retail sales" while adding that "even ~30 years in ('26) it's still only 28%."
Meta will be the first hyperscaler to reveal quarterly financials during this tech earnings cycle, with Alphabet , Microsoft and Amazon slated to report next week.
The four companies combined have called for roughly $730 billion in capital expenditures this year as they stock up on graphics processing units and AI systems and look to build massive data centers around the globe .
Analysts polled by FactSet expect that number to hit around $1 trillion next year, led by Alphabet, which is projected to spend over $310 billion. The stepped up spending comes as interest rates soar and concerns intensify that AI revenue won't justify the costs.
Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to report earnings next Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday.
Meta's past quarter wasn't all AI agents and good vibes.
The social media giant agreed in August to pay nearly $17 billion to settle a major lawsuit involving a group of state attorneys general, including California's Rob Bonta. The trial centered around allegations that Meta misled the public about the true scope of child mental health related harms caused by certain design elements of apps like Facebook and Instagram , including recommendation algorithms.
Meta's state AG settlement could cause the company to miss on third-quarter earnings per share due to the related $10 billion legal charge that "the street has not yet accounted for," Wolfe Research analysts wrote in a Monday note.
The company still faces numerous personal injury claims and a separate federal case involving a group of nationwide school districts that also focus on allegations that apps like Instagram have had detrimental effects on the well being of children.

articles.title_orig: What We Saw at Fast-Track Trials of Riot Suspects in France
articles.title_zh: What We Saw at Fast-Track Trials of Riot Suspects in France
articles.content_orig:
Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders
Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.
Months away from key elections in Spain, France and Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.
Those in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-right National Rally (RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.
The party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader, Marine Le Pen , said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.
Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.
In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.
Weidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”
In Portugal, populists have used peaceful protests to blame immigration for the country’s housing crisis, which André Ventura of the far-right Chega party said was chiefly a consequence of an “uncontrolled influx of people from abroad”.
In Spain, where the housing crisis has led to huge protests and a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap election next month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”
Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked the mammoth protests would have had a home had she been an immigrant from north Africa.
In Belgium , where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni , has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.
“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”
after newsletter promotion
Meloni has previously enacted sweeping security measures aimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.
This week she passed emergency decrees creating an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on ⁠rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.
Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.
Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”
The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.
Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.
JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.
Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: AT&T Stock Drops as Starlink Fears Overshadow Earnings. What It Means for the Dividend.
articles.title_zh: AT&T Stock Drops as Starlink Fears Overshadow Earnings. What It Means for the Dividend.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Stankey sees low-Earth-orbit satellites as a potential way to extend connectivity in rural areas rather than replace terrestrial wireless networks.
AT&T reported a 5.3% increase in quarterly revenue to $32.3 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $0.65.
The company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to about $2.40 and expects at least $18 billion in free cash flow.
AT&T (T) CEO John Stankey told analysts on Wednesday that investors shouldn't read too much into SpaceX's plan to become a mobile carrier during the company's third-quarter earnings call.
"I wouldn't over-rotate on what I would call one carrier of low-band spectrum."
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
SpaceX (SPCX) said this month, and confirmed on its second earnings call since going public on Tuesday, that it plans to turn Starlink into a major U.S. mobile carrier and is buying a block of low-band spectrum to do it.
T stock fell over 4% in morning trade and was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits alongside SPCX stock, which rallied over 8%. T stock pared losses after momentarily hitting a fresh three-month low at market open.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around T-Mobile improved to 'neutral' from 'bearish' territory over the past day. Meanwhile, sentiment around Elon Musk-led SpaceX jumped to 'extremely bullish' from the 'neutral' zone.
AT&T's third quarter (Q3) call also marked Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Pascal Desroches' last earnings call. Deputy CFO Jennifer Byry is set to take over after the new year.
Stankey said AT&T operates "somewhere between six to eight carriers of low-band spectrum" in a typical metropolitan area. According to him, a wireless network's performance depends on more than its spectrum holdings, pointing to the infrastructure needed to deliver service inside buildings, stadiums and hospitals.
He cited that in a city such as Chicago, 40% to 45% of mobile traffic originates indoors, where satellite signals face greater challenges.
"It takes a lot of years and a huge level of investment" to build a network that can deliver that level of performance, he said, adding that about 98% of the traffic is where AT&T already offers coverage.
Stankey did not dismiss satellite connectivity altogether. He said low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites are "fantastic for delivering bandwidth to rural areas" and could help AT&T serve sparsely populated areas more economically while reducing customer losses at the edges of its network.
Stankey said he expects "some kind of a peak and then a downward trajectory" for fixed wireless adoption. He said the most durable customer proposition is "a fiber-fed broadband customer with a great wireless service on top of it."
AT&T reported a record quarter for internet net additions across fiber and fixed wireless. The company also said its fiber network is well positioned to serve growing demand from data centers and cloud providers.
Stankey said more than 90% of mapped U.S. data centers are within 10 miles of AT&T's fiber network. Amazon Web Services (AWS) uses AT&T to connect its sites, and the carrier is working with Microsoft (MSFT) on high-capacity connectivity needs.
"Our fiber reach has never been greater. Our spectrum position has never been stronger."
AT&T's reported Q3 revenue rising 5.3% to $32.3 billion, above the roughly $31.65 billion consensus estimate as per Koyfin. Earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.65, compared to Wall Street's estimates of about $0.60. The company added 379,000 postpaid phone customers, with churn at 0.92%.
AT&T also raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to about $2.40 from a previous range of $2.25 to $2.35. The company expects adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) growth toward the upper end of its 3% to 4% range and free cash flow of at least $18 billion, including about $6 billion in the fourth quarter (Q4).
The telecom giant lowered its planned annual capital spending for 2027 and 2028 to $22 billion to $23 billion, a reduction of about $1 billion. It continues to target more than 60 million fiber locations by 2030.
Near-term pressures remain. Executives said during the earnings call that higher marketing and customer acquisition costs, along with about $100 million in vendor dispute settlements, are expected to weigh on Q4 EBITDA. They added that fiber revenue per customer fell 4% and is expected to decline by a similar amount, while home internet net additions are expected to slow during the holiday period.
On Stocktwits, message volume around T stock more than doubled over the past day. Retail traders debated the drop in shares despite an earnings beat and guidance raise.
One retail trader argued that AT&T shares appeared oversold and pushed back on comparisons with SpaceX, pointing to the cost and maintenance required to operate a satellite network at scale.
AT&T shares have fallen nearly 9% this year and almost 15% in the last 12 months.

articles.title_orig: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in its second round of job cuts this year
articles.title_zh: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in its second round of job cuts this year
articles.content_orig:
EBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce in a move to streamline its operations and focus on its fastest-growing areas, a company spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. The layoffs will affect approximately 1,000 employees.
"As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said in a statement.
The company also said it will continue to hire in "priority areas aligned with our strategy." As of the end of 2025, eBay had roughly 12,300 employees.
Reuters first reported the news, citing a memo to staff from CEO Jamie Iannone that read in part, "Our strategy is working."
"Continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest," Iannone said in the memo, seen by Reuters.
This is the second round of layoffs for the online marketplace this year, following a 6% workforce reduction that affected about 800 employees, in February. The company has been steadily shrinking its headcount over recent years at the same time it's ramping up spending on artificial intelligence.
EBay also acquired the used clothing resale platform Depop — a brand with a strong customer base of Gen Z and millennial users — from Etsy earlier this year. The $1.4 billion deal was finalized in July .
Shares of eBay were up approximately 1% Wednesday morning.
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Nearly $1 million worth of rare Pokemon and sports cards stolen from FedEx truck in Orange County heist, police say
articles.title_zh: Nearly $1 million worth of rare Pokemon and sports cards stolen from FedEx truck in Orange County heist, police say
articles.content_orig:
SANTA ANA, Calif. (KABC) -- Nearly $1 million in rare trading cards, including highly valued Pokémon cards, were stolen from a FedEx truck parked near an Orange County business that authenticates and grades the collectible items, according to police.
The theft is the latest in a string of heists involving Pokémon cards, which have exponentially increased in value in recent years.
The Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement on Tuesday that the heist occurred on Oct. 13 outside the Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) office in Santa Ana.
The hundreds of stolen cards are estimated to be worth a total of $963,000, according to police.
"However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined," according to the Santa Ana police statement.
The cards belong to collectors from across the country who submitted them to the PSA to be authenticated and graded.
Two full pallets of collectible cards were stolen, and some cards on a third pallet were also swiped when thieves broke into a FedEx truck, according to police.
"The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokémon cards," according to the police statement.
Thieves carve hole through drywall to steal high-value Pokémon cards from Anaheim shop
As of Wednesday, no arrests have been announced in the memorabilia rip-off. Police said the investigation is ongoing.
"The value is definitely there," said Gregory Lawrence of Shiny Vault Pokémon Cards. "It's another asset class now. It's not just stocks, bonds, and putting money in the bank. You can put money into cards. Whether it's Pokémon or sports, there is a huge following from across the world."
The theft was first reported by The Athletic, which cited police sources saying the the FedEx truck was broken into during the 60 to 90 minutes the driver was away from the parked vehicle.
"We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items. We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues," Collectors, the parent company of PSA, said in a statement to ABC News.
The company said it deactivated the certificates for the missing cards and has notified its "marketplace partners to be on the lookout for rare and serialized items."
"Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value," the company said. "We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset."
FedEx released a statement to ABC7, saying, "The security of our customers' shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation. Further questions should be referred to local investigators."
One victimized collector, known by his online handle, Sky-B Cards, issued a YouTube video statement , saying the 104 cards he submitted to PSA for grading were among the stolen items. He said he paid more than $8,000 to have the cards graded by PSA and that his cards were insured for more than $150,000.
"These were 104 cards that I've accumulated over two years," Sky-B Cards said in the YouTube video. "There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again, and honestly that's what hurts the most, outside of being absolutely financially destroyed here."
The heist is the latest in a string of thefts in Southern California and elsewhere in the country of highly valued Pokémon cards, highlighting what appears to be an ever-growing demand for merchandise from the popular childhood card game.
In February, thieves broke into a collectibles shop in Anaheim, by cutting a hole through the wall from a neighboring shop they also broke into, stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of Pokémon cards.
Captured on video surveillance cameras, the three thieves were seen grabbing hundreds of trading cards and bolting from the shop in less than 10 minutes.
In April, thieves staged a smash-and-grab heist at Elite Sports Cards in Chicago, stealing $100,000 in Pokémon cards, the store owner told ABC Chicago station WLS.
In an interview in April, Jared Mast, president of Mast Wealth Management Group, which deals in alternative investments including collectibles like Pokémon cards, told ABC News the value of Pokémon cards has risen sharply in the past year.
"I would say, collectively, over the last 12 months, things have gone up anywhere from 200 to 300%," Mast said.
Mast explained that Pokémon card value has risen in three different waves over the last decade. First, in 2016, with the arrival of Pokémon Go, the popular mobile game based on the playing cards, and then again in 2019 and 2020, as a generation of celebrities like Logan Paul invested in the collectibles.

articles.title_orig: Websites taken down across Europe as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.title_zh: Websites taken down across Europe as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.content_orig:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X , Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are " temporarily down for maintenance " without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. They used state-of-the art AI, made by OpenAI, to find the flaws.
OpenAI said in a blog post it was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
According to the firms, they had gone undetected for more than a decade.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note .
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning .
"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.
"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".
The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title_orig: DOJ official takes swipe at United Airlines CEO amid backlash over wealth tax proposal
articles.title_zh: DOJ official takes swipe at United Airlines CEO amid backlash over wealth tax proposal
articles.content_orig:
Dagen McDowell slams United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby over his proposal for a national wealth tax and a near-100% inheritance tax. She calls out the double taxation and points to the hypocrisy of the airline's own elite status pricing.
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby is facing criticism over his support for a national wealth tax and inheritance taxes approaching 100%, with a senior Justice Department official joining the backlash by taking a jab at the airline's service.
Harmeet K. Dhillon, assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, weighed in on the controversy with a post on X about her recent experience flying United.
"The WiFi didn’t work on my last two flights," Dhillon wrote.
Her comment followed Kirby's remarks in a recent interview with The New York Times , in which he warned that growing wealth inequality poses a "danger" to American society.
UNITED CEO SILENT ON $32M COMPENSATION AFTER CALLING WEALTH GAP A ‘DANGER’
Harmeet K. Dhillon speaks at the IAC National Summit 2026 at The Diplomat Beach Resort on January 17, 2026, in Hollywood, Florida.
"We should have a national wealth tax — it won’t work by state because people will just move," Kirby told the Times. "And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100 percent at some level. I would pay them."
Scott Kirby, chief executive officer at United Airlines Holdings Inc., during a Bloomberg Television interview at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) in Newark, New Jersey, US, on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Kirby's position has also drawn attention to his own compensation. The United CEO received about $32.3 million in total compensation in fiscal year 2025, including salary, stock awards and performance incentives. That was roughly 334 times the $96,670 median employee compensation reported by the airline, according to United's 2026 proxy statement.
FORMER UNITED EXECUTIVE EXPLAINS HOW NEW JERSEY FIBER CUT DISRUPTED NORTHEAST FLIGHTS
Beyond his tax proposals, Kirby also addressed United's pricing practices during the interview, defending the airline's decision to charge passengers more for certain seating options.
"There are some customers who want to sit in a window seat or a better seat, and that costs money to deliver," Kirby said.
A United Airlines Boeing 757 departs from Los Angeles International Airport en route to New York on Sept. 19, 2024, in Los Angeles, California. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images / Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
His comments prompted criticism from some social media users, with some threatening to stop flying United and others urging Kirby to focus on ticket prices and customer service.
One user wrote that Kirby should focus on "Flight safety, price, timeliness," adding, "How about we start with not charging $500 for basic 2 hour domestic routes?"
FOX Business' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in push to simplify operations, internal memo shows
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in push to simplify operations, internal memo shows
articles.content_orig:
EBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce in a move to streamline its operations and focus on its fastest-growing areas, a company spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. The layoffs will affect approximately 1,000 employees.
"As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said in a statement.
The company also said it will continue to hire in "priority areas aligned with our strategy." As of the end of 2025, eBay had roughly 12,300 employees.
Reuters first reported the news, citing a memo to staff from CEO Jamie Iannone that read in part, "Our strategy is working."
"Continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest," Iannone said in the memo, seen by Reuters.
This is the second round of layoffs for the online marketplace this year, following a 6% workforce reduction that affected about 800 employees, in February. The company has been steadily shrinking its headcount over recent years at the same time it's ramping up spending on artificial intelligence.
EBay also acquired the used clothing resale platform Depop — a brand with a strong customer base of Gen Z and millennial users — from Etsy earlier this year. The $1.4 billion deal was finalized in July .
Shares of eBay were up approximately 1% Wednesday morning.
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.title_zh: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.content_orig:
Earlier this month AMD senior vice president Jack Huynh told media in South Korea that FSR 4 was coming to more devices, including handhelds - and now that promise has been fulfilled.
Huynh today announced that FSR 4.1 was coming to five new platforms: Radeon RX 6000-series graphics cards; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo mini PCs and mobile workstations; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo Ryzen 9 laptops; Z2 Extreme and Z2A handhelds like ROG Xbox Ally devices; and Xbox Series X and Series S.
It's a welcome surprise to see AMD's latest generation upscaler on a huge range of extra devices - even though community modders have been working hard to port the technique to an even longer list of supported platforms.
FSR 4, previously known as Project Redstone, is AMD's first machine learning upscaler and offers a significant visual advantage over its earlier efforts at similar frame-rates - hence the interest in making it available on a wider range of PCs, handhelds and other devices. As well as upscaling and anti-aliasing, the tech also includes frame generation and ray reconstruction, giving it better feature parity with Nvidia's similar DLSS tech.
Huynh's announcement also states that FSR is coming to Vulkan, a graphics API that is the default choice for games that don't use (or want to offer an alternative to) DirectX 12. FSR 3 and earlier supported Vulkan, so it's good to see this limitation redressed - though it's not clear how quickly developers will be able to add FSR 4.1 support to their Vulkan games.
More APUs will get FSR 4.1 support in the future, Huynh claimed, and the announcement video also mentions that AMD's next-gen FSR Diamond will be supported on Xbox's Project Helix " family of devices ".
If you want to use FSR 4.1 on your PC (officially) for the first time, you'll need to install Adrenalin Edition version 26.10.1 . The graphics drivers also add support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Final Fantasy Resonance.

articles.title_orig: Inside Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4: The New Game-Changing Tech Powering Every Mode
articles.title_zh: Inside Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4: The New Game-Changing Tech Powering Every Mode
articles.content_orig:
Infinity Ward recently opened its Krakow research and development centre to us to showcase the technical advancements powering Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Infinity Ward Poland studio head Michal Drobot was on hand to present debug footage that explained how current-gen hardware on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and PC enables unprecedented visual and systemic upgrades. While a Nintendo Switch 2 version is also launching in parallel via Digital Legends, the core engine focus remains firmly on pushing broader performance and graphical boundaries - including ray-marched smoke and fog, revamped rasterisation techniques informed by path tracing, and a comprehensively reworked animation and movement system.
Let's start with one of the standout additions, a brand new volumetric ray-marched smoke and fog system built exclusively for MW4. Working in tandem with traditional transparencies, this voxel-based solution allows players to interact directly with smoke plumes using gunfire or vehicles. Bullets carve precise temporary holes through the volume - as in Counter-Strike 2 - while sprinting characters displace wisps naturally, all operating within a fixed GPU performance ceiling.
This unified voxel framework extends seamlessly across atmospheric elements, height fog, and overhead clouds, ensuring consistent competitive balance across all online multiplayer and DMZ modes. Server and local client synchronisation guarantees that visual interactions such as lighting, shadows, and smoke dispersion appear identically for every participant. Furthermore, volumetric fog self shadows and interacts dynamically with animated light sources within the environment.
Weather systems also benefit heavily from the new voxel architecture, supporting dynamic transitions between sunshine, rainfall and snow across expansive open maps - a huge change for open-ended modes like DMZ. Snow layers accumulate dynamically on top of existing level geometry, allowing players to gradually reveal the original terrain beneath. Additionally, expanded character and object voxels now track more environmental states than previous games - a great range of variables that coats soldiers in mud, dust, blood or water streaks depending on their movement.
Next there's the new material workflow used in Modern Warfare 4. While full path tracing is reserved for internal visual reference only due to its heavy performance cost - and RT global illumination and RT reflections are PC-exclusive features - MW4 developers chose to heavily optimise rasterisation pipelines, achieving visual results remarkably close to path tracing at a fraction of the computational expense. This strategy ensures the game easily maintains a high frame-rate across a much wider spectrum of hardware, a key consideration given how much of Call of Duty's audience plays on console with 60fps in mind.
A core component of this improved rasterised approach is the neural light grid, which leverages machine learning compression to handle dynamic ambient occlusion and global illumination, a rethought approach that seeks to avoid the typical artefacts caused by screen-space reflections (SSR) and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO). By storing lighting data more efficiently, light probes can be distributed sparsely across levels without sacrificing visual fidelity. Incidentally, it's an innovation that also helps to reduce the game's installation sizes alongside improved texture streaming techniques.
In part, material rendering receives a major upgrade through custom capture hardware known as the ATVI CT Reflectometer 2.0. By capturing physical surface properties across multiple light gradients, artists are able to access accurate bidirectional reflectance distribution function values for skin, clothing and metallic surfaces. This new material workflow integrates well with the enhanced rasterised ambient occlusion and global illumination passes.
Under the hood, significant optimisations target the entire rendering pipeline through advanced variable rate shading. Variable rate shading dynamically compresses visual data in less critical areas while preserving full native resolution where it matters most, drastically reducing overall graphical overhead - and this time, it's now applied throughout the entire render pipeline, not just for the final rendered pixels. Additional efficiency is gained through multi-resolution transparencies, with effects like smoke scaling in resolution based on distance.
Supporting these techniques, a hybrid rendering setup is also in place: combining traditional forward rendering (F+) with a visibility buffer (V+) for dense geometry. Where it's efficient to do so, parts of the scene will flip from one to the other, with F+ tending to handle triangles nearer the player.
Finally, foundational gameplay mechanics have been completely overhauled alongside these more visual-focused upgrades. Character movement directly influences weapon sway and contextual interactions with walls, while a new physical bullet trajectory simulation replaces older random bloom mechanics.
Together with these technical engineering achievements, Modern Warfare 4 stands as one of the more significant series milestones. It refines the experience for long term fans of the franchise - and impressions from the early access period suggest the campaign at least is one of the series' best in recent memory. We'll have more to say on Modern Warfare 4 to come, including the Switch 2 edition, but for now the outlook on the game's tech is promising to say the least.
